plan: Humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000059), an original essay on linear perspective: Brunelleschi's Baptistery panel and mirror (c. 1415), Alberti's On Painting, Panofsky's 1927 'symbolic form', and the author's balanced view (exact geometry, conventional standard). Written to test whether a denser argumentative passage with a balanced authorial position raises blind-rated difficulty. No perspective passage in any bank. Ten questions, six aimed at hard. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The Single Eye
passages.text:
Sometime around 1415, the Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi stood in the doorway of the unfinished cathedral and painted a small panel of the octagonal Baptistery across the square. What he did next is better remembered than the painting, which has not survived. He drilled a hole through the panel at the point toward which the building's receding lines converged, and he invited viewers to look through the hole from the back, at a mirror held in front of the painted side. Seen this way, from a single fixed position, the reflected image was said to be hard to tell apart from the building itself.

The demonstration is usually told as the moment when painters discovered how vision works. Within two decades the humanist Leon Battista Alberti had set down a method in his treatise On Painting, describing the picture as a window through which the viewer looks at the scene, and the rules of linear perspective spread through the workshops of Italy and then of Europe. In the familiar telling, earlier painters had simply been wrong about space, and the Renaissance corrected them.

That telling is not false, but it is incomplete. In a 1927 essay, the art historian Erwin Panofsky called perspective a "symbolic form," by which he meant that it expresses a particular way of conceiving the world rather than a neutral record of it. The system rests on assumptions that no actual viewer meets: a single eye rather than two, an eye that does not move, and a visual field that is flat rather than curved. Brunelleschi's peephole is revealing precisely because it enforces those assumptions. The illusion succeeds only when the viewer is made to see as the system requires.

None of this makes perspective arbitrary. Its geometry is exact: given the position of an eye and a flat picture plane, the place where each point of a scene should appear can be calculated. What is conventional is the decision to treat that single, motionless eye as the standard of truth. Medieval painters who enlarged a saint or showed the inside and outside of a building at once were not failing to see; they were answering a different question, about importance or about what a viewer needed to know, rather than about how a scene would look from one spot.

The distinction matters because conventions, once learned, become invisible. A modern viewer who finds a fourteenth-century altarpiece "flat" or "naive" is judging it by rules that were themselves invented, however well they were founded. To see Brunelleschi's mirror clearly is to see both achievements at once: a precise solution to a problem of projection, and a quiet redefinition of what a picture is for.

candidates.stem: The main idea of the passage is that linear perspective:

choices.A: was invented to correct painters who had misunderstood how vision works.
choices.B: is an arbitrary system that has no more claim to accuracy than medieval methods.
choices.C: is geometrically exact yet rests on conventions about how a picture should represent seeing.
choices.D: succeeded mainly because Brunelleschi's demonstration was so hard to tell from reality.

candidates.evidence: None of this makes perspective arbitrary.
candidates.explanation: The author grants that perspective's geometry is exact but argues that treating one motionless eye as the standard of truth is a convention, so the system is both a solution and a redefinition.

A.rationale: This is the "familiar telling" that the author calls incomplete.

B.rationale: The author says perspective is not arbitrary and that its geometry is exact.

D.rationale: The demonstration is the starting point, not the explanation the passage offers for perspective.

hints: How does the author qualify the familiar telling?

strategy.explanation: Find where the author agrees and where the author disagrees with the usual account.

candidates.remember: A main idea must include the author's qualifications.

author_checklist.hardness: Two distractors each capture one half of the author's balanced position.

candidates.stem: The main function of the second paragraph is to:

choices.A: present a common account that the author goes on to qualify.
choices.B: explain the geometry that makes perspective exact.
choices.D: argue that Alberti misunderstood Brunelleschi's method.

candidates.evidence: In the familiar telling, earlier painters had simply been wrong about space
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 sets out the usual story; paragraph 3 begins "That telling is not false, but it is incomplete."

B.rationale: The geometry is discussed in paragraph 4.

C.rationale: The demonstration is described in paragraph 1.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests that Alberti misunderstood anything.

hints: What does paragraph 3 say about "that telling"?

strategy.explanation: Read the first sentence of the next paragraph.

candidates.remember: A paragraph's function often shows in how the next one responds.

candidates.stem: The author would most likely agree that the medieval painters described in the fourth paragraph:

choices.A: could not see space accurately until perspective was discovered.
choices.B: painted more accurately than artists who used linear perspective.
choices.C: were unaware that saints could be shown at natural size.
choices.D: made choices suited to purposes other than showing one viewpoint.

candidates.evidence: they were answering a different question
candidates.explanation: The author says the medieval painters "were not failing to see; they were answering a different question," about importance or what a viewer needed to know.

A.rationale: The author says they "were not failing to see."

B.rationale: The author does not rank their accuracy above perspective's; they answered a different question.

C.rationale: The author presents enlarging a saint as a choice about importance, not ignorance.

hints: What does "a different question" refer to?

strategy.explanation: Reread the last sentence of paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: Separate what an author explains from what an author ranks.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must avoid both the old 'failure' view and an overcorrection that ranks medieval art higher.

candidates.stem: The author describes Brunelleschi's peephole as "revealing" (paragraph 3) mainly because it:

choices.A: allowed viewers to compare the painting directly with the real Baptistery.
choices.B: shows that the illusion works only when the viewer sees as the system assumes.
choices.C: proved that Brunelleschi understood the geometry better than Alberti did.
choices.D: revealed a flaw in Brunelleschi's painting that a mirror could correct.

candidates.evidence: The illusion succeeds only when the viewer is made to see as the system requires.
candidates.explanation: The peephole fixes one eye at one position, the very assumptions on which perspective rests; that is why the author calls it revealing.

A.rationale: Comparison is part of the demonstration, but the author's point is about the fixed single eye the peephole imposes.

C.rationale: The passage never compares their understanding.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests a flaw; the mirror was part of the viewing arrangement.

hints: What assumptions does the peephole enforce?
candidates.remember: Ask why the author chose a particular word.

author_checklist.hardness: The obvious reading (comparison with the real building) is not the author's point.

candidates.stem: As it is used in the third paragraph, the word neutral most nearly means:

choices.A: neither positive nor negative in charge.
choices.B: not taking a side in a dispute between nations.
choices.C: free of any particular point of view.

candidates.evidence: rather than a neutral record of it
candidates.explanation: Panofsky contrasts "a particular way of conceiving the world" with a "neutral record," so "neutral" means not shaped by any particular viewpoint.

A.rationale: This is a scientific sense of "neutral" that does not fit a record of the world.

B.rationale: This political sense does not fit a description of how pictures record the world.

D.rationale: This sense applies to colors, not to a way of recording a scene.

strategy.explanation: Use the contrast with "a particular way of conceiving the world."

candidates.remember: Use the sentence's contrast to pick the right sense.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which assumption of linear perspective does no actual viewer meet?

choices.A: The viewer looks with a single eye that does not move.
choices.B: The viewer stands inside the building being painted.
choices.C: The viewer looks at a curved rather than a flat picture.
choices.D: The viewer sees the scene reflected in a mirror.

candidates.evidence: a single eye rather than two, an eye that does not move
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists the assumptions: a single eye, an eye that does not move, and a flat visual field.

B.rationale: Brunelleschi stood in the cathedral doorway, but this is not one of the assumptions listed.

C.rationale: The passage says the system assumes a flat visual field, not a curved picture.

D.rationale: The mirror was part of one demonstration, not an assumption of the system.

hints: Find the list of assumptions in paragraph 3.
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the exact sentence.

candidates.stem: Which statement best captures the distinction the author draws in the fourth paragraph?

choices.A: Perspective's geometry is exact, so its standard of truth cannot be a convention.
choices.B: The geometry is exact, but making one fixed eye the standard is a convention.
choices.C: Medieval methods are exact in a different way, so perspective's geometry is a convention.
choices.D: Perspective is conventional because its geometry was invented by painters, not by scientists.

candidates.evidence: What is conventional is the decision to treat that single, motionless eye as the standard of truth
candidates.explanation: The author holds two claims together: the geometry is exact, and the choice of a single motionless eye as the standard is conventional.

A.rationale: The author separates the exact geometry from the conventional standard; one does not rule out the other.

C.rationale: The author calls perspective's geometry exact, not conventional.

D.rationale: The author says the geometry is exact; who invented it is not the point.

hints: Which part does the author call exact, and which conventional?
candidates.remember: Track which claim an author attaches to which part of an idea.

author_checklist.hardness: Each distractor merges or swaps the two halves of the distinction.

candidates.stem: The author suggests that a modern viewer who calls a fourteenth-century altarpiece "naive" is:

choices.A: correctly identifying painters who lacked technical skill.
choices.B: using the same standards that fourteenth-century viewers used.
choices.C: rejecting the idea that perspective has an exact geometry.
choices.D: applying learned rules without recognizing that they are rules.

candidates.explanation: Because conventions become invisible once learned, the modern viewer judges the altarpiece by rules "that were themselves invented" without noticing them.

A.rationale: The author argues that such painters were answering a different question, not lacking skill.

B.rationale: The modern viewer judges by perspective, which came later.

C.rationale: The modern viewer takes perspective for granted rather than rejecting it.

hints: What does the author say happens to learned conventions?

strategy.explanation: Read the first sentence of the last paragraph.

candidates.remember: Look for the cause the author gives for a judgment.

candidates.stem: The author's attitude toward Brunelleschi's achievement is best described as:

choices.A: admiring of its precision while alert to what it quietly assumes.
choices.B: dismissive, because it relied on a trick with a mirror.
choices.C: uncritically celebratory, because it revealed how vision works.
choices.D: indifferent, because the original painting has not survived.

candidates.evidence: a precise solution to a problem of projection, and a quiet redefinition of what a picture is for
candidates.explanation: The final sentence praises the achievement as "a precise solution" and also calls it "a quiet redefinition," so the author both admires it and notices its assumptions.

B.rationale: The author calls it a precise solution, which is not dismissive.

C.rationale: The author says the celebratory account is incomplete.

D.rationale: The lost painting is mentioned, but the author engages closely with the achievement.

hints: How does the last sentence describe the achievement?

strategy.explanation: Look for both praise and qualification.

candidates.remember: Balanced attitudes need balanced answer choices.

author_checklist.hardness: The key combines admiration and critique; distractors take one extreme.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Alberti's treatise described a picture as:

choices.A: a mirror that reflects a building back to the viewer.
choices.B: a window through which the viewer looks at a scene.
choices.C: a symbol of the painter's way of conceiving the world.
choices.D: a record of what a viewer needed to know about a building.

candidates.evidence: describing the picture as a window
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says Alberti described the picture as a window through which the viewer looks at the scene.

A.rationale: The mirror belongs to Brunelleschi's demonstration, not to Alberti's description.

D.rationale: That describes the medieval painters' purpose in paragraph 4.

hints: Who said what? Match each idea to its source.

strategy.explanation: Find Alberti's name and read that sentence.

candidates.remember: Keep track of which source holds which idea.
